```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
library(here)
library(tidyverse)
here::i_am("errata.qmd")

t4 <- read_csv(here("maintained", "output", "table_4_vote_share_precinct.csv"),
               show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(model == "Model 1", term == "Z")
b3 <- read_csv(here("maintained", "output", "table_b3_vote_share_precinct_cd.csv"),
               show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(term == "Z")
```

This note lists four errors in "Does digital advertising affect vote choice? Evidence from a randomized field experiment," published in *Research & Politics* 9(1), doi [10.1177/20531680221076901](https://doi.org/10.1177/20531680221076901). **None of them changes a conclusion of the paper.** They are recorded because the numbers themselves are wrong and a reader who quoted them would be misled.

Item 1 is a misstated number in the text. Items 2 through 4 are errors in the appendix: two of labelling, one of a table printed in place of another. Every corrected value below is computed from the deposited replication archive ([10.7910/DVN/UH2NQW](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/UH2NQW)) at the time this document is rendered. The maintained code is at [github.com/active-maintenance-aec/coppock_green_porter_2022](https://github.com/active-maintenance-aec/coppock_green_porter_2022).

## 1. The unadjusted estimate is misstated by a factor of ten

Published, p. 5:

> ...a **2.1 percentage point** increase in Democratic vote share, though this estimate is uncertain, as evidenced by its large **standard error of 3.0 percentage points**.

Corrected:

> ...a **`r sprintf("%.2f", t4$estimate*100)` percentage point** increase in Democratic vote share, though this estimate is uncertain, as evidenced by its large **standard error of `r sprintf("%.2f", t4$std.error*100)` percentage points**.

Table 4 reports `r sprintf("%.4f", t4$estimate)` with a standard error of `r sprintf("%.4f", t4$std.error)`, and the next sentence applies percentage point units correctly to the adjusted estimate. The published standard error of 3.0 corresponds to no model in the paper or the appendix. The claim the sentence makes is unaffected: on either reading the unadjusted estimate is small and swamped by its standard error, and the paper's conclusion rests on the covariate-adjusted estimate in column 2, which is reported and interpreted correctly throughout. The error appears in the published version and in the preprint.

## 2. Figure G.2 names the wrong effect size

Published, panel annotation:

> Power when PATE = **0.1**

Corrected:

> Power when PATE = **0.01**

The simulated effects are drawn from a normal distribution centred at 0.01, which is what the appendix text says two paragraphs earlier. The label is a hardcoded string in the analysis script.

## 3. Covariate row labels are wrong in five appendix tables

Published, Tables E.7 and F.8, covariate row:

> **Two Party Vote Share**

Corrected:

> **Two Party Vote Margin**

Those models regress on lagged two-party vote *margins*, not shares.

In Tables F.9, F.10 and F.11 a vector of coefficient names one element shorter than the model shifts every covariate row from 2016 downward onto the label belonging to the row above it. The 2016 vote share coefficient is printed as **Missingness Indicator (2016)**. No coefficient is affected; only the labels are wrong.

## 4. Appendix Table B.3 reprints Table B.4

Table B.3 is captioned "Effects on vote share (CD fixed effects)." Every cell beneath that caption is identical to Table B.4, "Effects on vote margin (CD fixed effects)": the same coefficients, standard errors, R-squared values and covariate labels, all on the vote margin scale. The vote share models with congressional district fixed effects appear nowhere in the appendix.

Those models are estimable from the deposited data. The effect of any treatment video on vote share with district fixed effects is `r sprintf("%.4f", b3$estimate[1])` (`r sprintf("%.4f", b3$std.error[1])`) without covariates, the same substantive result as Table 4.
